So I'm not going to answer your meal question because I don't think that is the right question for you to be asking. Meal plans are for fat people who want to lose weight and don't care to actually learn how to eat, how to take care of themselves, or how to hold themselves accountable for their decisions. You were obese before you started to lose weight and you're asking for a meal plan, so it's likely that your attitude towards food is somewhat retarded.

To begin with, keep doing what you're doing because you still have a little ways to go as far as weight loss. What you've done has obviously worked so just keep that up.

Your attitude towards food needs to be this: FOOD IS FUEL. The idea that all food should taste good is hedonism that is pushed by advertising jews to get you to spend more money. We all understand that the purpose of gasoline is something other than to make smells that are pleasant to our nose, so we don't complain about how the gas station does not semll as pleasant as a rose. We all understand that the purpose of a cinderblock is something other than to provide a pleasant appearance to our eyes, so we don't complain about how a warehouse does not appear as pleasing as mahogany and gold.

The things that you put into your body are the fuel for the activities that you are going to perform with your body.

You should be thinking about different food like they're an algebraic equation of: Calories, portion size / satiety, hedonistic value, and macronutrients (aka carbs / protein / fats). Satiety is "how full does it make you feel" and hedonistic value is "how much do you enjoy eating it". I will usually also consider monetary cost as another variable, but that's not an inherent quality of the food itself but more like something to keep in mind since it will almost always factor into your consumption decisions.

For reference: there are 4 calories in each gram of carbohydrate, and sugar is a type of carbohydrate. There are also 4 calories in one gram of protein. One gram of fat has 9 calories in it.

I like to think of oatmeal as an example. I had really only ever considered eating the oatmeal packets and not plain oats until I read people talking about oats on /fit/. So let's really compare the two, assume that we're preparing it the same with the same amount of milk to eliminate that as a variable, here's a site about plain oats which includes the nutritional information, and here's a link to the nutritional information for Quaker oatmeal packets maple & brown sugar flavor. Look at the oatmeal packet, one serving size is 43 grams and of that 43 grams, 12 GRAMS is sugar. Compare it to the amount of sugar in plain oats, clearly it's ADDED sugar so of that 43g in a packet, 12 of it is added sugar. There's also "salt" in the ingredientsbut 260mg sodium translates to only .65grams of salt so we're basically talking about 30g of oats, 12 grams of sugar, plus a tiny bit of salt and flavoring in each packet of oatmeal.

If you normally eat two packets that's only 60g of oats and 24g of sugar. A tablespoon of sugar is 12g, so even if you made 60g of plain oats and added one tablespoon of sugar, you'd still be saving yourself 48 calories that were doing nothing for you nutritionally. What I have found is that I eat plain oats so quickly that I don't really get any hedonistic value from adding any sugar to it at all. I can cook up a cup of plain oats, add a little milk to cool it down and thin it out, and eat it all in less than a minute. For reference a cup of plain oats is about 90 grams, which is the amount of actual oats that are in 3 oatmeal packets.

Now let's go back to that algebraic equation and decide which thing we want to make the same to compare the two foods - calories is the easiest because it's actually measurable. Two oatmeal packets is 320 calories. 82g of plain oats is 320 calories. I am much less hungry after I eat 82g of plain oats than I am when I eat the oatmeal packets (60g of plain oats + 24g sugar). I get slightly more hedonistic value from the sugar, but I eat it so quick that it's not much, and I would gain much more hedonistic value from other things instead. It's clear to me that plain oats are a better use of my calories.

Now macros are maybe a little ahead of where you need to be but it's good to keep in mind whether calories are coming from fat protein or carbs. Fat and protein are preferable to carbs. Oats has lots of carbs so if you eat two eggs and half a cup of plain oats you'll have a good macro balance, you'll be good and filled up and you'll feel like a fucking king to start the day. Be careful about the amount of oil or butter you use. That should be no more than 400 calorie breakfast and it will be nutritionally rock solid. Additional bonus: it will take you like 5 minutes to make, and it will cost you less than $.50. There's 1/3 of your meal plan, eat this every fucking day.

As far as your workout goes, I'd say start doing compound lifts. It sounds like you're probably lifting with machines. Get some reps in doing bench press, squats, and deadlifts. You don't have to do it super heavy right now because in order to lose weight you have to eat fewer calories than you burn so you won't be building much muscle anyway. The point is to make sure you have the proper form down and the balancing muscles built up a bit so that by the time you get your weight down to like 155 or 160 you are ready to switch to a much more lifting-intensive routine. At that point maybe whittle down the cardio to like 20 minutes at the end of your lifting session and eat a little more so you're at just a little bit of a caloric deficit from where you were before. Those three compound lifts will be the most important ones so do those first. Machines are shit for building muscle on their own. Stop eating at a caloric deficit when your body fat composition gets low enough that you feel you're healthy and that the main thing holding back your lifting session is that you feel too fatigued (as opposed to feeling too weak, you'll learn the difference). Keep a lifting journal where you track what lift you did, how heavy, and how many reps / sets. New page every day take it with you to every station and write it down when you're done with your exercise so you don't forget.

Also to elaborate on this, the "satiety" and "hedonistic value" factors are how you find some foods that are calorically dense end up being good for you. Peanut butter, nuts, whole milk and avocados are some things that are good for you and denser in calories than other things, but they end up being better for you because of their nutritional qualities and because they fill you up more. Skim milk has fewer calories than whole milk but it's pretty thin. 200 calories of whole milk will be less, but it will fill you up more than 200 calories of skim milk. Drink water for your 2nd glass then intead of another glass of milk. Actually, always only drink water unless it's black coffee or milk that you planned in, or booze that you're working into whatever your "junk food allowance" is.

This is also the easiest way that I've found to add good calories back into your diet. You don't change the way you've been eating when transitioning off a calorie-deficit, just add a few calorie dense things in. Two tablespoons of peanut butter in your oatmeal is +190cal. Slice up half an avocado on your sandwich at lunch is +120cal. A quarter cup of mixed nuts mid-afternoon is +150 cal, and 1 cup additional of whole milk at dinner is +150 cal. That's 600 calories right there to move you from a caloric-deficit diet of 1800 to a more sustained 2400 cal diet, if you're lifting hard enough to support it. The best part about those 4 changes is that they have a good ratio of macros for that kind of a transition.
